title: Poetic syntax and morphology

objectives.can: Read poetic lines that omit a verb, the article, אֵת or אֲשֶׁר, and recognise poetic forms and word order.
concepts: qatal and yiqtol in parallel lines

explanation.summary: Hebrew poetry is compressed. A verb in one line serves two; small words like the article, אֵת and אֲשֶׁר are often left out; the verb forms and word order are freer than in narrative; and a handful of older or longer forms appear. Knowing these habits lets you read a line without being puzzled by what is missing.

sections.heading: One verb for two lines
body: The commonest kind of compression is ellipsis: a word is stated in one line and understood in the next. It is usually the verb, and sometimes a negative with it. In Psalm 1:5 the second line has no verb of its own. In Psalm 121:6 the second line, וְיָרֵחַ בַּלָּיְלָה, 'and the moon by night', takes the verb and the negative from the first line: 'the sun will not strike you by day, nor the moon by night'.

Deuteronomy 32:2 shows it at greater length. The first two lines have verbs, 'my teaching drops like rain, my speech flows like dew'. The next two have none, so they borrow: 'like showers on the grass, and like downpours on the herb'. When a line looks short, ask which word of the previous line is doing double duty.

sections.heading: Small words that poetry often leaves out
body: In prose a definite object usually has אֵת before it, a noun that is definite usually has the article, and a relative clause begins with אֲשֶׁר. In poetry all three are used much less, as a general tendency, and a reader must supply them. In Deuteronomy 32:3 the object שֵׁם יְהוָה has no אֵת: 'I will call the name of the LORD'. In Deuteronomy 32:17 the clause אֱלֹהִים לֹא יְדָעוּם is a relative clause with no אֲשֶׁר: 'gods whom they did not know'.

The tendency is not a rule. The article does appear in poetry: Deuteronomy 32:4 begins הַצּוּר, 'the Rock'. And poetry has its own relative word: זוּ in Exodus 15:13, עַם זוּ גָּאָלְתָּ, 'the people whom you redeemed'.

sections.heading: Word order and verb forms
body: Word order is freer in poetry than in prose. A poet may put the object first, as in Psalm 19:2, or set a subject before everything, then take it up again with a pronoun. In Psalm 23:4 the speaker names שִׁבְטְךָ וּמִשְׁעַנְתֶּךָ, 'your rod and your staff', and then says הֵמָּה יְנַחֲמֻנִי: the pronoun picks the pair up and stresses it.

Verb forms alternate in parallel lines with no change of time. In Psalm 23:5 the first line has the yiqtol תַּעֲרֹךְ and the second line has the qatal דִּשַּׁנְתָּ. In Exodus 15:5 the first line has a yiqtol, יְכַסְיֻמוּ, and the second a qatal, יָרְדוּ. A reader should not hunt for a change of time. The poet is varying the form, and the two lines speak of one event or one habit. Whether such a verb is past, present or future comes from the context.

sections.heading: Poetic and old forms
body: A number of forms stand mostly in poetry, and some of them look old. Learn to recognise them, but do not read them as different in meaning from the ordinary form.

The suffix -מוֹ is a longer form of the ending 'them'. The prepositions עַל and אֶל have longer forms עֲלֵי and אֱלֵי. Some nouns in the construct state keep an old linking vowel; חַיְתוֹ in Isaiah 56:9 means 'beasts of' and the final vowel is not 'his'. And the ending -הוּ on a noun, as in וְעָלֵהוּ in Psalm 1:3, is a fuller spelling of the ordinary 'his'. A few words are rare enough that only their parallel line helps; you will meet that in the lessons on wisdom.

Ordinary form
Where
rows: the construct without a linking vowel

sections.heading: Figures of speech
body: Poetry says much by images. A simile compares with 'like' (the prefix כְּ). A metaphor says one thing is another: the Psalm 23 poet writes יְהוָה רֹעִי, 'the LORD is my shepherd', with no 'like'. A metonymy names a thing by something closely tied to it. A merism names two extremes to mean everything between them.

In Psalm 23:5, כּוֹסִי רְוָיָה, 'my cup is full', is often read as metonymy: the cup stands for what the host gives. In Psalm 121:8, צֵאתְךָ וּבוֹאֶךָ, 'your going out and your coming in', is a merism for all of a person's movements. Name the figure simply, and then ask what it says in the passage.

head: Figure
What it does
Where to look
rows: Names a thing by something tied to it
Two extremes stand for the whole

misunderstandings: A missing אֵת, article or אֲשֶׁר is not a mistake and is not a clue that the text is damaged. It is the ordinary compression of poetry, and a reader supplies the word.
A qatal in one line and a yiqtol in the next do not mean that the time changed. The poet is varying the form.
Poetic forms such as -מוֹ and עֲלֵי do not mean something other than the ordinary forms. They are longer or older spellings of the same words.
A figure of speech is not an ornament added to a plain statement. The image carries the meaning, and the reader should say what the image says before going to a plain paraphrase.

deeper.heading: Old poems and later poems
body: Exodus 15 and Deuteronomy 32 are often described as archaic poems because they hold many of the forms in this lesson. Scholars differ about how old they are and about whether such forms prove an early date or are a deliberate style kept by later poets. For a reader the practical lesson is the same: these forms are normal in poetry.

quoted.title: Deuteronomy
quoted.english: My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew; as the small rain upon the tender grass, and as the showers upon the herb.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two lines with verbs, יַעֲרֹף and תִּזַּל, each with a simile (כַּמָּטָר, כַּטַּל). The third and fourth lines have none: כִּשְׂעִירִם עֲלֵי דֶשֶׁא and וְכִרְבִיבִים עֲלֵי עֵשֶׂב borrow the verbs. The preposition עֲלֵי is the longer poetic form of עַל.

quoted.title: Deuteronomy
quoted.english: For I will proclaim the name of the LORD; ascribe ye greatness unto our God.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: שֵׁם יְהוָה is the object of אֶקְרָא, 'I will call', and it has no אֵת. Prose would usually mark a definite object like this one with אֵת. Its absence here is a mark of poetic style.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: Then will He speak unto them in His wrath, and affright them in His sore displeasure:
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The long preposition אֵלֵימוֹ means the same as אֲלֵיהֶם, 'to them', and the verb יְבַהֲלֵמוֹ carries the same -מוֹ as its object, 'it will terrify them'. The ending -מוֹ stands for the third person plural.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies; Thou hast anointed my head with oil; my cup runneth over.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: A yiqtol in the first line, תַּעֲרֹךְ, and a qatal in the second, דִּשַּׁנְתָּ, with no change of time: both describe the shepherd's care as host. The last line, כּוֹסִי רְוָיָה, is a nominal clause, and the cup stands for what the host gives.

quoted.title: Deuteronomy
quoted.english: They sacrificed unto demons, no-gods, gods that they knew not, new gods that came up of late, which your fathers dreaded not.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: אֱלֹהִים לֹא יְדָעוּם is a relative clause with no אֲשֶׁר: 'gods whom they did not know'. The next words, חֲדָשִׁים מִקָּרֹב בָּאוּ, 'new ones that came lately', are another relative clause without a relative word. Prose would normally put אֲשֶׁר before both.

practice.prompt: The third and fourth lines of this verse (כִּשְׂעִירִם עֲלֵי דֶשֶׁא וְכִרְבִיבִים עֲלֵי עֵשֶׂב) have no verb. Where does it come from?

quoted.title: Deuteronomy
quoted.english: My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew; as the small rain upon the tender grass, and as the showers upon the herb.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: From a verb in the next verse
From the verbs of the first two lines, יַעֲרֹף and תִּזַּל
From the preposition עֲלֵי, which is itself a verb
From nowhere: the lines are broken
practice.explain: Poetry lets one verb serve more than one line. The verbs of the first two lines carry on into the next two, so the sense is 'my teaching drops like showers on the grass' and so on.

options: The two forms are varied in the two lines, and the time comes from the context, not from the change
The second line must be earlier than the first
The second line is a command
The first line must be future and the second past

options: It picks up the fronted pair, 'your rod and your staff', and gives them stress
practice.explain: The poet places the two things first and then says, 'they, they comfort me'. The pronoun sums up the pair and gives it weight. This is a freedom of word order that poetry allows.

check.prompt: What figure of speech is יַעֲרֹף כַּמָּטָר לִקְחִי?

quoted.title: Deuteronomy
quoted.english: My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew; as the small rain upon the tender grass, and as the showers upon the herb.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A simile: the prefix כַּ, 'like', compares the teaching to rain
check.explain: A comparison that uses 'like' is a simile. The next line, תִּזַּל כַּטַּל אִמְרָתִי, 'my speech flows like the dew', makes another.

check.prompt: What figure is יְהוָה רֹעִי, 'the LORD is my shepherd'?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: A Psalm of David. The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A metaphor: it says the LORD is a shepherd, with no 'like'
check.explain: There is no word for 'like' and no verb. The clause is a nominal clause and says that the LORD is the speaker's shepherd. The whole psalm then unfolds the image.

check.prompt: What is the figure in צֵאתְךָ וּבוֹאֶךָ, 'your going out and your coming in'?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: The LORD shall guard thy going out and thy coming in, from this time forth and for ever.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A merism: two extremes stand for all of a person's movements
check.explain: Going out and coming in are the two ends of a journey. Together they mean everything a person does. The verb יִשְׁמָר serves both: the LORD will guard both.

check.prompt: The first line has the yiqtol תַּעֲרֹךְ and the second line has the qatal דִּשַּׁנְתָּ. How should a reader take this?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies; Thou hast anointed my head with oil; my cup runneth over.

options: As a change from future to past
As a mistake in the text
As a variation of the verb form in parallel lines, the two lines speaking of the same care
As a change from past to future
check.explain: Poetry varies the form of a verb in parallel lines without a change of time. The context, the shepherd's present care, decides how to put the verbs in English.

check.prompt: What would prose normally put before לֹא יְדָעוּם in the clause אֱלֹהִים לֹא יְדָעוּם?

quoted.title: Deuteronomy

quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

check.explain: The clause describes the gods: 'gods that they did not know'. A relative clause in prose would begin with אֲשֶׁר. Poetry often leaves it out.

check.prompt: What does זוּ do in עַם זוּ גָּאָלְתָּ?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: Thou in Thy love hast led the people that Thou hast redeemed; Thou hast guided them in Thy strength to Thy holy habitation.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It is a verb meaning 'to flow'
It is a relative word, like אֲשֶׁר: 'the people whom you redeemed'
check.explain: In poetry זוּ can introduce a relative clause, as in this song. The corpus analyses it as a relative conjunction. The clause says who the people are: those whom the LORD redeemed.

check.prompt: What is אֱלֵי in הַשְּׂמֵחִים אֱלֵי גִיל?

quoted.title: Job
quoted.english: Who rejoice unto exultation, and are glad, when they can find the grave? —
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A longer poetic form of the preposition אֶל, 'to, toward'
check.explain: The long form אֱלֵי is a poetic variant of אֶל. The phrase means something like 'who rejoice to the point of exultation'. The word is not a divine name here.

check.prompt: In כֹּל חַיְתוֹ שָׂדָי the ending of חַיְתוֹ looks like 'his'. How does the phrase read?

quoted.title: Isaiah
quoted.english: All ye beasts of the field, come to devour, yea, all ye beasts in the forest.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: 'Every one of them' of the field
'All the beasts' with the final vowel marking a question
'All the beasts of the field', with the final vowel an old linking vowel of the construct state
check.explain: The word is in the construct state before שָׂדָי. The final -וֹ is an old ending that a few nouns keep in poetry, and there is no 'his' here. The corpus analysis agrees: it gives a construct state and no suffix.

check.prompt: What is the ending on וְעָלֵהוּ in 'its fruit in its season, and its leaf does not wither'?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: And he shall be like a tree planted by streams of water, that bringeth forth its fruit in its season, and whose leaf doth not wither; and in whatsoever he doeth he shall prosper.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A fuller spelling of the ending 'his'
check.explain: The ending -הוּ is the third person masculine singular suffix, 'his', in a fuller form than the plain -וֹ of פִּרְיוֹ and בְּעִתּוֹ in the same verse. The leaf is 'its leaf', that is the tree's leaf.

reading.why: A short psalm full of the features of the lesson: a metaphor that governs the whole poem (23:1), yiqtol and qatal in parallel (23:5), a fronted pair taken up by a pronoun (23:4), a figure in the closing line, and many places where a line is short because the previous line supplies its verb. The heading belongs to verse 1.

segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

sources: Gesenius' Hebrew Grammar, ed. E. Kautzsch, tr. A. E. Cowley, 2nd English edition (1910), poetic forms and the suffix -מוֹ
G. B. Gray, The Forms of Hebrew Poetry (1915), the forms of Hebrew poetry
S. R. Driver, A Treatise on the Use of the Tenses in Hebrew, 3rd edition (1892), the tenses in poetry

authoring.by: Written for Ecclesia by Claude (Anthropic), following the public-domain grammars listed as sources. Every Hebrew word shown as an example, in a paradigm or in an exercise is taken from the Westminster Leningrad Codex as analysed by the Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible project.
